### 4.3.1 – Introducing (y = mx + b)

* Every non-vertical line can be written as (y = mx + b) or (f(x) = mx + b).
* These two equations mean the **same thing** — (f(x)) just reminds us that y depends on x.
* (m) is the **slope** (how fast y changes).
* (b) is the **y-intercept** (the starting value when (x = 0)).

:::{.think title="Why is (b) special?"}
When (x = 0), (y = b).
That’s the point ((0, b)) — where the line crosses the y-axis.
:::

:::{.real-world title="Example – A Taxi Ride"}
A taxi charges $3 to start plus $2 per mile.
The rule is (y = 2x + 3) or (f(x) = 2x + 3).

* (m = 2): you pay $2 per mile (the rate).
* (b = 3): you start at $3 before any miles are driven.
  :::

:::{.you-try title="Find the starting value"}
For (f(x) = 5x + 2), what does the 2 represent in context?
:::

### 4.3.2 – Graphing Using Slope and Intercept

1. Plot the y-intercept ((0, b)).
2. Use the slope (m = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}) to find another point.
3. Draw a line through the points.

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_3/graph_from_slope_intercept.png){width="340px" fig-align="center"}

:::{.think title="Direction Matters"}
A positive slope goes **up to the right**; a negative slope goes **down to the right**.
:::

:::{.you-try title="Graph (f(x) = –2x + 4)"}
Start at (0, 4), then go down 2 and right 1 to find the next point. Connect the dots.
:::

---

### 4.3.3 – Changing (m) and (b)

* Changing **(m)** changes the **steepness** or direction.

  * Larger (m) → steeper line.
  * Negative (m) → line falls left to right.
* Changing **(b)** moves the line **up or down** but keeps the same tilt.

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_3/change_m_b_effect.png){width="360px" fig-align="center"}

:::{.real-world title="Comparing Cell Plans"}
Two cell phone plans:

* **Plan A:** (y = 30x + 10)
* **Plan B:** (f(x) = 20x + 25)

Which is cheaper for small x? Which is cheaper for large x?
:::

:::{.real-world title="Where Two Rules Are Equal"}
Two plans are given by  
\(f(x) = 30x + 10\) and \(g(x) = 20x + 25\).  

Graph both on the same axes.  
The point where the lines **intersect** shows when both plans cost the same —  
one (x, y) pair that works for **both** equations.
:::

:::{.you-try-m title="Predict the change"}
If we increase (b), what happens to the graph?
If we make (m) negative, what happens?
:::

---

### 4.3.4 – (y) and (f(x)): Two Ways to Write the Same Rule

* (f(x)) is just another way to write (y).
* Mathematicians use (f(x)) to show that y **depends on** x — it’s the same rule written differently.

:::{.think title="Evaluating (f(x))"}
If (f(x) = 2x + 3), then (f(4) = 2(4) + 3 = 11).
That means the point ((4, 11)) is on the line.
:::

:::{.remember title="Key Idea"}
(y = mx + b) and (f(x) = mx + b) describe the **same linear function**.

* (m) tells the **rate of change** (slope).
* (b) tells the **starting value** (y-intercept).
  Together, they describe how the line looks and what it means.
  :::
